result.content:
# Phishing Domain Investigation Playbook
## Target: `suspicious-site.example`

> **Prerequisites:** Install `whois`, `dnsutils` (dig), `jq`, `chromium` (or `google-chrome`), and set your VirusTotal API key in env var `VT_API_KEY`.
> Run everything from a dedicated directory:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/phishing-investigation/suspicious-site.example && cd ~/phishing-investigation/suspicious-site.example
```

---

## STEP 1 — WHOIS Lookup

**(1) Command:**
```bash
whois suspicious-site.example | tee whois.txt
```

**(2) Save to:** `whois.txt`

**(3) Grep for:**
```bash
grep -iE 'registrant|creation_date|expiration_date|registrar|name_server|status' whois.txt
```

**(4) What to look for → Next step depends on:**
| Finding | Interpretation | Next Step |
|---|---|---|
| Domain created < 30 days ago | **High suspicion** — phishing domains are often very recently registered | Proceed to Step 2, flag as `NEW_DOMAIN` |
| Registrar is known-bulletproof (e.g., `TUCOWS`, `NAMECHEAP` with no abuse policy) | Moderate suspicion | Proceed to Step 2 |
| Registrant email is a random Gmail/Yandex/ProtonMail | **High suspicion** — legitimate businesses use corporate domains | Proceed to Step 2, flag as `ANONYMOUS_REGISTRANT` |
| Domain has `clientTransferProhibited` and valid registrant | Lower suspicion | Proceed to Step 2 normally |

---

## STEP 2 — Passive DNS & Subdomain Discovery

**(1) Command:**
```bash
# Query multiple public DNS resolvers + subdomain enumeration via crt.sh
dig suspicious-site.example ANY +noall +answer > dns_any.txt 2>&1
dig suspicious-site.example A +short > dns_a.txt 2>&1
dig suspicious-site.example MX +short >> dns_a.txt 2>&1
dig suspicious-site.example TXT +short >> dns_a.txt 2>&1
dig suspicious-site.example NS +short >> dns_a.txt 2>&1
# Passive DNS via crt.sh (certificate transparency — also surfaces subdomains)
curl -s "https://crt.sh/?q=%25.suspicious-site.example&output=json" | jq -r '.[].name_value' 2>/dev/null | sort -u > subdomains.txt
# Also try SecurityTrails (requires free API key — optional)
# curl -s -H "APIKey: $ST_API_KEY" "https://api.securitytrails.com/v1/domain/suspicious-site.example/dns_records" | jq . > securitytrails_dns.json
```

**(2) Save to:** `dns_any.txt`, `dns_a.txt`, `subdomains.txt`

**(3) Grep for:**
```bash
echo "=== A Records ===" && cat dns_a.txt
echo "=== Subdomains found ===" && cat subdomains.txt
echo "=== TXT records (SPF/DKIM/verification) ===" && grep -iE 'v=spf1|v=DKIM|v=DMARC|google-site-verification|MS=|facebook-domain-verification' dns_a.txt
echo "=== Suspicious name servers ===" && grep -iE 'ns1\.cheap|ns2\.cheap|cloudflare-nginx|ns\.digitalocean|ns\.hostinger|ns\.godaddy' dns_a.txt
```

**(4) What to look for → Next step depends on:**
| Finding | Interpretation | Next Step |
|---|---|---|
| A record resolves to a known-bulletproof IP (check via `grep -f known_bad_ips.txt dns_a.txt`) | **High suspicion** | Proceed to Step 3, flag `MALICIOUS_IP` |
| Subdomains found like `login.suspicious-site.example`, `admin.suspicious-site.example`, `secure.suspicious-site.example` | **Phishing pattern** — subdomains mimicking login portals | Proceed to Step 3, flag `PHISHING_SUBDOMAINS` |
| No A record / NXDOMAIN | Domain may be parked or not yet active | Proceed to Step 3 anyway (may be pre-deployment) |
| TXT records show legitimate business verification (e.g., Google, Microsoft) | Lower suspicion | Proceed to Step 3 normally |

---

## STEP 3 — Certificate Transparency (CT) Log Analysis

**(1) Command:**
```bash
curl -s "https://crt.sh/?q=suspicious-site.example&output=json" | jq -r '.[] | [.id, .name_value, .issuer_name, .not_before, .not_after, .pem_certificate] | @tsv' 2>/dev/null > ct_logs.tsv
# Also extract unique domains covered by any cert
curl -s "https://crt.sh/?q=suspicious-site.example&output=json" | jq -r '.[].name_value' 2>/dev/null | sort -u > ct_domains.txt
# Extract the actual certificate PEM for the primary domain
curl -s "https://crt.sh/?q=suspicious-site.example&output=json" | jq -r '.[0].pem_certificate' 2>/dev/null > cert.pem 2>/dev/null
```

**(2) Save to:** `ct_logs.tsv`, `ct_domains.txt`, `cert.pem`

**(3) Grep for:**
```bash
echo "=== All domains in CT logs ===" && cat ct_domains.txt
echo "=== Issuer ===" && grep -iE 'issuer' ct_logs.tsv
echo "=== Certificate validity window ===" && grep -iE 'not_before|not_after' ct_logs.tsv
echo "=== SANs (Subject Alternative Names) ===" && cat ct_domains.txt | grep -iE 'login|secure|account|verify|update|paypal|amazon|microsoft|google|apple|bank|chase|wells|citibank|coinbase|binance'
echo "=== Self-signed or weak issuer ===" && grep -iE 'self-signed|Let'\''s Encrypt' ct_logs.tsv
```

**(4) What to look for → Next step depends on:**
| Finding | Interpretation | Next Step |
|---|---|---|
| CT cert covers `login-suspicious-site.example` or `suspicious-site.example` with a brand name in SANs | **Phishing indicator** | Proceed to Step 4, flag `BRAND_SPOOFING_CERT` |
| Certificate issued by Let's Encrypt with no OV/EV validation | Common for phishing (free, automated) | Note but not conclusive — proceed to Step 4 |
| Certificate issued by DigiCert/Sectigo with verified org name matching a real company | Could be legitimate or could be a stolen cert | Proceed to Step 4, flag `VERIFIED_ISSUER` for deeper review |
| No CT records found | Domain may be too new or not yet serving HTTPS | Proceed to Step 4 |

---

## STEP 4 — HTTP/HTTPS Probe

**(1) Command:**
```bash
# Full verbose HTTP probe (follow redirects, show headers, show body snippet)
curl -svL --max-time 15 --output page_content.html --dump-header response_headers.txt \
  -w "\nHTTP_CODE:%{http_code}\nREDIRECT_URL:%{url_redirect}\nSIZE:%{size_download}\nTIME:%{time_total}\n" \
  https://suspicious-site.example 2>&1 | tee http_probe.txt
# Also probe on HTTP (port 80) in case HTTPS is misconfigured
curl -svL --max-time 15 --output page_content_http.html --dump-header response_headers_http.txt \
  -w "\nHTTP_CODE:%{http_code}\nTIME:%{time_total}\n" \
  http://suspicious-site.example 2>&1 | tee http_probe_http.txt
# Check response headers for suspicious indicators
cat response_headers.txt
```

**(2) Save to:** `http_probe.txt`, `page_content.html`, `response_headers.txt`, `http_probe_http.txt`, `page_content_http.html`, `response_headers_http.txt`

**(3) Grep for:**
```bash
echo "=== HTTP Status Code ===" && grep 'HTTP_CODE' http_probe.txt
echo "=== Suspicious Headers ===" && grep -iE 'server|x-powered-by|x-aspnet-version|set-cookie|location|refresh|content-security-policy|strict-transport-security' response_headers.txt
echo "=== Login/Form indicators in HTML ===" && grep -iE '<form|action=.*login|password|username|sign.in|sign.in|verify.account|update.payment|card.number|cvv|suspicious.activity|account.suspended|verify.your.identity|click.the.link|urgent' page_content.html
echo "=== Brand names in page content ===" && grep -iE 'paypal|amazon|apple|google|microsoft|bank of america|chase|wells fargo|citibank|coinbase|binance|netflix|facebook|twitter|instagram|linkedin' page_content.html
echo "=== Redirect to another domain ===" && grep -iE 'location:|redirect' response_headers.txt
echo "=== JavaScript obfuscation ===" && grep -iE 'eval\(|atob\(|String\.fromCharCode|document\.write' page_content.html
echo "=== HTTP status on plain HTTP ===" && grep 'HTTP_CODE' http_probe_http.txt
```

**(4) What to look for → Next step depends on:**
| Finding | Interpretation | Next Step |
|---|---|---|
| Page contains login forms with brand names (PayPal, Apple, etc.) | **Confirmed phishing** | Proceed to Step 5, flag `CONFIRMED_PHISHING` |
| HTTP 200 with brand impersonation content | **Confirmed phishing** | Proceed to Step 5, flag `CONFIRMED_PHISHING` |
| HTTP 301/302 redirect to a different domain | Possible redirect chain phishing | Proceed to Step 5, note the redirect target |
| HTTP 403/404/503 | Site may be down or blocking scanners | Proceed to Step 5 anyway (try screenshot) |
| No content at all (empty body) | Domain may be parked | Proceed to Step 5 to confirm |

---

## STEP 5 — Screenshot

**(1) Command:**
```bash
# Chromium headless screenshot (full page)
chromium --headless --no-sandbox --disable-gpu --screenshot=screenshot.png --window-size=1920,1080 https://suspicious-site.example 2>/dev/null
# If chromium not available, try:
# google-chrome --headless --no-sandbox --disable-gpu --screenshot=screenshot.png --window-size=1920,1080 https://suspicious-site.example 2>/dev/null
# Fallback: save the HTML as a visual reference
cp page_content.html page_content_backup.html
```

**(2) Save to:** `screenshot.png`

**(3) Grep for:** (visual inspection — no grep, but verify the file exists and has content)
```bash
ls -la screenshot.png && file screenshot.png && echo "Screenshot size: $(stat --c%s screenshot.png) bytes"
# If screenshot is very small (< 5KB), it's likely an error page or blank page
grep -q 'error\|404\|blocked\|captcha' page_content.html && echo "WARNING: Page may be blocking automated access"
```

**(4) What to look for → Next step depends on:**
| Finding | Interpretation | Next Step |
|---|---|---|
| Screenshot shows a login page mimicking a brand | **Confirmed phishing** | Proceed to Step 6, flag `VISUAL_CONFIRMATION` |
| Screenshot shows a blank/error page | Site may be inactive or blocking | Proceed to Step 6 with whatever content was captured |
| Screenshot shows a CAPTCHA or Cloudflare challenge | Site is actively defending against analysis | Proceed to Step 6, note `ANTI_BOT_PROTECTION` |

---

## STEP 6 — Content Hash & Comparison

**(1) Command:**
```bash
# SHA-256 hash of the downloaded page content
sha256sum page_content.html > content_hash.txt
echo "SHA256: $(cat content_hash.txt)"
# Also hash the screenshot
sha256sum screenshot.png >> content_hash.txt
# If you have multiple phishing samples, compare against known phishing hash databases
# Check against PhishTank database
curl -s "https://checkurl.phishtank.com/checkurl/?url=suspicious-site.example" -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" -d "url=suspicious-site.example&format=json" 2>/dev/null | jq . > phishtank_check.json 2>/dev/null
# Also compute hash of the HTTP response body for comparison
cat page_content.html | sha256sum | awk '{print $1}' > body_hash.txt
```

**(2) Save to:** `content_hash.txt`, `phishtank_check.json`, `body_hash.txt`

**(3) Grep for:**
```bash
echo "=== Content SHA256 ===" && cat body_hash.txt
echo "=== PhishTank result ===" && cat phishtank_check.json 2>/dev/null
grep -iE 'in_database|
